title: Raga Kalyan
hookLine: the dishes are done, the lights come on, and the Granth turns to an evening raga that opens with a child and a parent

lines: THE LAST PLATE IN THE RACK.
cards: The last plate goes in the rack. Somebody switches on a lamp. Outside, the streetlights are on.

The day's noise has moved off into the next street: a kettle, a television low in another room, a child being called in. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga that tradition sings in this hour, as night begins.
Its name is Kalyan, and it opens with a family picture.

teach.h: AFTER KANARA: GURU RAM DAS, GURU ARJAN.
teach.b: In the Granth's order, Kalyan comes right after Kanara, and its pages hold hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan. Tradition places it in the first part of the night and calls its mood calm and settled.
Teachers of raga describe moods in different ways, so hold that as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. What is written is the opening hymn, by Guru Ram Das.

teach.h: NO ONE HAS FOUND THE LIMIT.
teach.b: In paraphrase: no one has found the limit of the Lord who is in everything.
We are your children; you are the one who looks after us. You are the great Being, my father and my mother. Notice the move.
The first line goes as big as it can: no limit, no end anyone has reached. The very next breath comes all the way home. Children.
A father. A mother. The infinite and the kitchen table, side by side.
Evening is the hour when children are called in, when whoever looks after a house counts heads and closes the door. The hymn hangs the whole of creation on that ordinary scene.
Whatever the day was, the one who sustains it is described as a parent. Peace, in this opening, isn't silence or emptiness. It's the feeling of a child who knows someone is watching the door.
Sikhs who sing Kalyan in the evening sing it into exactly the hour when that picture is easiest to see.

how: In kirtan, shabads from the Kalyan section, by Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, are sung in Raga Kalyan, which tradition associates with the evening.

games.why: the hymn turns straight from the limitless to the family: the one who sustains us, described as a parent.

practice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Kalyan; it doesn't need to be evening where you are, and if you can't, simply sit in the quiet.
Then call the day's pieces in one by one, the way someone calls children in from the street, the meeting, the errand, the thing you said too fast, and let the door close behind each.
If you pray, rest in Guru Ram Das's picture of the One who looks after us like a father and a mother; if you don't, let the house of your mind go quiet.

wordCard.voice: Raga Kalyan. The raga that follows Kanara, which tradition sings as night begins, opening with Guru Ram Das's hymn: no one has found your limit, and we are your children. Today's word.

orig.note: the raga's name as it appears in the Granth's heading, Raag Kalyan.
